claims.claim: Destination-driven autonomous flight and obstacle avoidance already exist commercially.
claims.finding: Skydio is a valid commercial example in supported missions and conditions. This establishes the capability exists, not equivalence across all brands or environments.

claims.claim: Skydio reliably avoids obstacles as small as a half-inch wire.
claims.finding: The manufacturer safety guide warns against wires and branches smaller than 0.5 inch. A stated minimum-object limitation is not a guaranteed wire-detection specification.

claims.claim: Skydio uses multiple cameras and real-time predictive autonomy.
claims.finding: Multi-camera navigation is documented. Do not infer architecture details, performance guarantees or universal moving-obstacle avoidance from “predictive AI.”

claims.claim: Pathfinder routes around terrain, buildings and geofences.
claims.finding: Pathfinder uses geospatial information for route planning. Cached map routing cannot account for every new crane, wire or moving object; it complements onboard avoidance.

claims.claim: Skydio can retain obstacle avoidance at night with NightSense.
claims.finding: NightSense is dedicated illumination hardware for supported aircraft/configurations. Ordinary passive-camera performance at night is not the same capability.

claims.claim: DJI waypoint + APAS actively bypasses obstacles rather than braking.
claims.finding: Mavic 4 Pro User Manual v1.2 §4.5 says waypoint flight brakes for obstacles whether Bypass or Brake is selected. APAS behavior is mode- and model-dependent.
claims.why: This is a direct contradiction for the specific model Grok named.

claims.claim: Mavic 4 Pro has omnidirectional vision plus LiDAR.
claims.finding: Omnidirectional visual sensing and forward-facing LiDAR are documented. Do not describe it as omnidirectional LiDAR.

claims.claim: Docked/enterprise systems support remote mission execution.
claims.finding: Commercial remote/docked operations exist. Remote operation, mission planning and sensed avoidance are separate capabilities with model-specific limits.

claims.claim: Avoidance may fail with wires, transparent surfaces, weather or moving obstacles.
claims.finding: Manufacturer limitations support this caution. Grok’s broad reference to dynamic avoidance must be checked per model; Skydio’s guide describes static-obstacle avoidance.

claims.claim: Navigation can run without continuous manual piloting, while oversight remains a separate requirement.
claims.finding: Grok explicitly included this distinction in its caveat. Autonomous route execution does not establish unattended arbitrary-environment operation; operator responsibilities and permitted operations are separate questions.

claims.claim: BVLOS and related rules can still require pilots/observers.
claims.finding: Directionally correct and jurisdiction-dependent. US Part 107 is one example with pilot/VLOS requirements and exceptions; this is not a statement of Jordanian or worldwide law.

claims.claim: Skydio’s core autonomy is closed; SymForce is open.
claims.finding: Supporting open libraries and integration APIs are distinct from an open release of the commercial navigation stack.

claims.claim: DJI is completely closed, with no source available.
claims.finding: Core APAS/firmware algorithms are proprietary. DJI also publishes SDK source; “completely closed” is too broad when applied to its whole ecosystem.

claims.claim: PX4 and ArduPilot are BSD/GPL open autopilots with missions and external control.
claims.finding: PX4 is BSD-3-Clause; ArduPilot GPL-3.0. Both supply control and mission foundations with different external-control and avoidance interfaces.

claims.claim: PX4 Avoidance is a suitable current companion-planner option.
claims.finding: The repository was archived in August 2024. The associated path-planning interface is unsupported and was removed in PX4 v1.15.

claims.claim: Both autopilots provide basic collision prevention.
claims.finding: Directionally correct, but the capabilities differ. PX4 collision prevention is distinct from ArduPilot BendyRuler detours in AUTO/GUIDED/RTL; Dijkstra+BendyRuler combines fence routing and sensed-obstacle avoidance.

claims.claim: Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner can supply local obstacle-avoiding trajectories.
claims.finding: They are real planners with public code and flight research. They require map/sensor-state inputs and a controller; neither is an autopilot or turnkey full product.

claims.claim: OctoMap/Voxblox and VIO/SLAM packages are useful perception building blocks.
claims.finding: Correct at the architectural level. Occupancy/distance maps and pose estimators solve different problems. OpenVINS/VINS/ORB-SLAM3 do not automatically supply a dense collision map; frames, timing and representations must agree.

claims.claim: ROS/ROS 2 plus MAVLink or DDS connects companion perception/planning to flight control.
claims.finding: This is a common architecture. MAVROS bridges MAVLink; PX4’s ROS 2 interface uses its compatible DDS path. ROS versions and setpoint/state contracts are not automatically compatible.

claims.claim: Jetson, Raspberry Pi or NUC can run companion autonomy.
claims.finding: All are plausible compute classes; feasibility depends on sensing, model, rates and power. A Pi cannot be assumed to run every stack at target speed. Small PULP-Dronet shows Jetson is not universally mandatory.

claims.claim: PX4 is currently the most common foundation for this work.
claims.finding: The reviewed examples make PX4 a reasonable and frequent choice. No defined population, survey or adoption measurement was supplied to justify the superlative.

claims.claim: Almost always start by assembling disparate projects yourself.
claims.finding: Many reusable integrated systems already perform substantial assembly. Choose between adopting a reference stack and composing components; integration effort remains in both.

claims.claim: Integration means drivers, map/trajectory interfaces, tuning and calibration—not random copying.
claims.finding: Correct. Concrete interface issues include frame conventions, sensor timestamps/extrinsics, odometry rates, map semantics and controller setpoints. Integrated releases reduce this work rather than eliminating it.

claims.claim: px4_fast_planner has already combined planner and autopilot components.
claims.finding: Actual integration source exists, with Fast-Planner and MAVROS controller dependencies. The inspected head is from 2020; it should not be presented as a maintained modern full stack.

claims.claim: No-GPS Autonomous Drone System already wires everything together; launch files exist.
claims.finding: The inspected default branch contains only README.md and LICENSE. No implementation or launch files support this claim.

claims.claim: CERLAB is a real integrated CMU autonomy system.
claims.finding: Verified nine module repositories and real navigation/exploration examples. The perception-to-control description needs the qualification that a suitable pose/odometry source is an external input.

claims.claim: NTNU Unified Autonomy Stack is an integrated open system.
claims.finding: Real code, workspace manifests and a 2026 paper support the claim. It is a newer public wrapper, mixes ROS versions, and exposes alternative modules rather than one mandatory pipeline.

claims.claim: OmniNxt provides integrated perception, planning and control.
claims.finding: Paper and assembly guide support a real reference system. The tiny root repository points to external branch-specific implementations; it is not self-contained.

claims.claim: Agilicious is a freely open-source full obstacle-avoidance stack.
claims.finding: The framework is real, but current core access is governed by an academic agreement. Control/hardware framework and related obstacle-avoidance experiments are not the same release.

claims.claim: Aerostack2-based setups belong among modular end-to-end autonomy frameworks.
claims.finding: The framework is real, and a chosen setup can combine the required stages. This does not establish default general 3D avoidance: the inspected A* plugin uses a 2D occupancy map and needs an appropriate perception/planning configuration.

claims.claim: MRS already integrates the pieces.
claims.finding: A substantial deployed flight framework with optional estimation/mapping/planning modules. Current ROS 2 migration status matters; some ROS 1 modules are not yet ported.

claims.claim: Altnautica adds the higher-level fly-here-and-avoid-stuff behavior.
claims.finding: Actual operational agent code exists. Vision navigation docs establish VIO/pose support, not a mature general 3D obstacle planner. Treat it as an operations platform, not a verified Skydio equivalent.

claims.claim: These public systems can fly real obstacle-avoiding missions.
claims.finding: Multiple papers and releases support real flight in specific setups. A paper demonstration, released code, reproducible deployment and product robustness are four different evidence levels.

claims.claim: None match Skydio in robustness, thin obstacles, night performance or polish.
claims.finding: No matched public comparison across those dimensions was supplied. SUPER reports thin-wire and night experiments, but compares a DJI Mavic 3 in the wire test—not Skydio. There is no justified universal ranking.

claims.claim: Most complete stacks require matching reference sensors and calibration.
claims.finding: Reference-stack documentation supports substantial hardware/configuration dependence. “Most” is qualitative here; no census was performed, and Jetson-class compute is not universal.

claims.claim: Starting from an assembled stack leaves adaptation rather than inventing the architecture.
claims.finding: A fair practical conclusion. Choose a stack whose sensors, license, ROS branch and task match your project, then validate the resulting system in your actual environment.
